query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behaviors of HfNbTaTiZr arise from an internally generated residual stress field that develops from a nanoscale thermal expansion mismatch between regions with enhanced lattice distortion (and/or early-stage precipitation) and a less-distorted matrix. This internal field acts to pin dislocations and counter thermal softening, thereby producing the high‐temperature strength plateau and unusual elastic modulus temperature dependence observed in separate tests.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast, single‐phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr with inherent lattice distortion and nanoscale heterogeneity.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled cold rolling and subsequent aging treatments to deliberately vary the extent of lattice distortion and nano‐precipitation, or alternatively introduce a minor alloying addition that minimizes differences in thermal expansion coefficients among local regions.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests (tensile creep, microhardness, and elastic moduli measurements) and thermal expansion experiments conducted over a wide temperature range (from room temperature up to ~1250 °C), with particular focus on the 873–1073 K region where strength and modulus plateaus are observed.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale heterogeneities (regions of higher lattice distortion and/or nano‐precipitates) that have a different coefficient of thermal expansion than the surrounding matrix, generating internal residual stresses during heating and cooling.
generation.mechanism: On heating, the differential expansion between the distorted/precipitate regions and the matrix produces internal residual stresses that effectively counteract the temperature‐driven ease of dislocation motion. This enhances dislocation pinning (and possibly modifies the activation energy for dislocation climb or glide) so that the yield strength and elastic moduli exhibit reduced temperature sensitivity (a plateau) despite the usual thermal softening. Conversely, treatments that reduce the thermal expansion mismatch would lead to conventional thermomechanical behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples in which the internal residual stress from thermal expansion mismatch is enhanced (or unaltered) will show a high-temperature strength/moisture plateau and an elevated elastic modulus over the 873–1073 K window, whereas samples engineered to reduce the mismatch (via minor alloying additions or alternative heat treatments) will exhibit a more typical continuous softening with temperature. Additionally, differences in dislocation arrangements and local strain fields (observable by TEM or XRD residual stress mapping) should correlate with the degree of lattice mismatch.
generation.baseline: The untreated, as‐cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy showing the previously reported stress–strain and thermoelastic behaviors.
generation.boundary: Temperature range from room temperature up to ~1250 °C (with a critical interest in the plateau region between 873 K and 1073 K) and deformation conditions spanning tensile creep, hardness testing after cold rolling, and aging-induced hardening.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of the thermal expansion mismatch relative to other factors (such as impurity interstitial effects, oxidation, and dynamic precipitate evolution) is not precisely known. It is also uncertain how microstructural evolution during thermal cycling might further modify the residual stress field over long times.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: (1) a control group with the standard processing (as‐cast followed by cold rolling/aging) to maintain the natural heterogeneity and thermal expansion mismatch, and (2) an experimental group modified by adding a minor element (or applying a tailored heat treatment) designed to homogenize the thermal expansion behavior across the microstructure. Subject both groups to tensile creep, microhardness, and elastic modulus measurements across the temperature range (with an emphasis on 873–1073 K). In parallel, use XRD and TEM to map residual stress fields and dislocation structures.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and creep rate as a function of temperature
Elastic moduli via resonant ultrasound spectroscopy or in situ neutron diffraction
Thermal expansion coefficients (and anisotropy) of different microstructural regions
Residual stress mapping through XRD or TEM
Microstructural characterization (e.g., nanoprecipitate distribution, lattice distortion) via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If reducing the thermal expansion mismatch (i.e., in the experimental group) does not lead to a measurable change in the temperature-dependent yield strength plateau, elastic modulus behavior, or dislocation structure relative to the control group, then the hypothesis that internal residual stresses from thermal expansion mismatch govern the anomalous mechanical behavior will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Overall, this comprehensive study provides evidence for the unique elastic and plastic deformation behavior of the single BCC solid-solution phase refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using in situ neutron experiments coupled with theoretical calculations. The results of the ND and characterization of the microstructure show the excellent BCC single-phase stability up to 900°C. Furthermore, the present alloy has the high yield strength and excellent plasticity at RT and softening resistance at elevated temperatures. The lattice strain evolution results show the distinctive elastic deformation behavior as an elastic isotropy at RT and less temperature dependency in the elastic anisotropic deformation behavior than conventional metallic materials at elevated temperatures. The single-crystal elastic moduli are obtained from the in situ ND data coupled with the Kroner model approach, showing excellent agreement with the experimental values determined from RUS measurements and first-principles calculations. Investigations of mechanical properties and microstructure of different MEAs derived from the HfNbTaTiZr alloy system has been performed. It has been shown that ductility is significantly reduced by simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy, which leads to reduction of the BCC1 phase content. These elements segregate during solidifying. Because of the miscibility gap in the Ta-Zr equilibrium phase diagram two BCC phases are found after cooling to room temperature. Clear correlation between the BCC1 phase content and the total elongation to failure of the alloy was found. Precipitation of Ta rich precipitates on grain boundaries reduces the elongation to almost zero values. No correlation was found between the tensile mechanical properties and microstructure related parameters in investigated set of alloys. The 5 element HEA alloy exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation. 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength to various extent. Some of them are ductile (NbTaTiZr, NbTaTi, NbTiZr) but some of them are brittle (TaTiZr, Nb1.5TaTiZr0.5, Nb0.5TaTiZr1.5) depending on microstructure.
